title: Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. RESULTS: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties ("Skin" best: 0.041; "Social & Preventive Medicine" worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. DISCUSSION: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. CONCLUSION: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved "self-knowledge", but uneven overconfidence persists.

claims.text: Mean Expected Calibration Error (ECE) across medical specialties ranged from 0.041 for 'Skin' to 0.141 for 'Social & Preventive Medicine'.
Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the lowest overall mean ECE of 0.06 among the six evaluated LLMs.
GPT-4o exhibited the highest overall mean ECE of 0.127 among the six evaluated LLMs.
GPT-5 achieved the highest mean accuracy of 91.1% across the evaluated medical specialties.
Gemini 2.5 achieved the second-highest accuracy (90.4%) but ranked fifth in calibration (mean ECE 0.094) due to systematic overconfidence.
Increasing model parameter size within the GPT-5 model series improved calibration performance.
High accuracy in large language models does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation.

limitations.text: Reliance on multiple-choice questions from MedMCQA may not capture LLM performance in open-ended clinical reasoning or real-world diagnostic scenarios.
Question difficulty and question style (e.g., fact recall vs. opinion-based) were not controlled or assessed in the dataset sample.
Only proprietary LLMs were evaluated; open-weights models were not tested.
Most prior work reports pooled calibration across domains, which obscures potentially large specialty-specific calibration differences.

future_work.text: Conduct formal hypothesis testing in future experiments to complement the descriptive analysis.
Incorporate domain- and specialty-specific calibration reporting into future LLM medical benchmarks alongside standard accuracy metrics.

methodologies.name: Self-reported confidence elicitation and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) analysis
methodologies.description: Evaluated accuracy and ECE across 20 medical specialties on 2,000 sampled MedMCQA questions per model using a two-step standardized prompt eliciting numerical confidence scores (0-100).
conditions: 2,000 questions sampled across 20 medical specialties (100 per specialty)
Models evaluated: GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5
Two-step prompting: answer generation followed by 0-100 confidence score elicitation
